refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: The /etc/machine-id file contains the unique machine ID of the local system that is set during installation or boot. The machine ID is a single newline-terminated, hexadecimal, 32-character, lowercase ID. When decoded from hexadecimal, this corresponds to a 16-byte/128-bit value. This ID may not be all zeros.

The machine ID is usually generated from a random source during system installation or first boot and stays constant for all subsequent boots. Optionally, for stateless systems, it is generated during runtime during early boot if necessary.

The machine ID may be set, for example when network booting, with the systemd.machine_id= kernel command line parameter or by passing the option --machine-id= to systemd. An ID specified in this manner has higher priority and will be used instead of the ID stored in /etc/machine-id.

The machine ID does not change based on local or network configuration or when hardware is replaced. Due to this and its greater length, it is a more useful replacement for the gethostid3 call that POSIX specifies.
This machine ID adheres to the same format and logic as the D-Bus machine ID.

This ID uniquely identifies the host. It should be considered "confidential", and must not be exposed in untrusted environments, in particular on the network. If a stable unique identifier that is tied to the machine is needed for some application, the machine ID or any part of it must not be used directly. Instead the machine ID should be hashed with a cryptographic, keyed hash function, using a fixed, application-specific key. That way the ID will be properly unique, and derived in a constant way from the machine ID but there will be no way to retrieve the original machine ID from the application-specific one. The sd_id128_get_machine_app_specific3 API provides an implementation of such an algorithm.

refsect1.title: Initialization
refsect1.para: Each machine should have a non-empty ID in normal operation. The ID of each machine should be unique. To achieve those objectives, /etc/machine-id can be initialized in a few different ways.
For normal operating system installations, where a custom image is created for a specific machine, /etc/machine-id should be populated during installation.
systemd-machine-id-setup1 may be used by installer tools to initialize the machine ID at install time, but /etc/machine-id may also be written using any other means.

For operating system images which are created once and used on multiple machines, for example for containers or in the cloud, /etc/machine-id should be either missing or an empty file in the generic file system image (the difference between the two options is described under "First Boot Semantics" below). An ID will be generated during boot and saved to this file if possible. Having an empty file in place is recommended because it allows a temporary file to be bind-mounted over the real file, in case the image is used read-only and when /etc is mounted read-only in the early boot. Also see Safely Building Images.
systemd-firstboot1 may be used to initialize /etc/machine-id on mounted (but not booted) system images.

When a machine is booted with systemd1 the ID of the machine will be established. If systemd.machine_id= or --machine-id= options (see first section) are specified, this value will be used. Otherwise, the value in /etc/machine-id will be used. If this file is empty or missing, systemd will attempt to use the D-Bus machine ID from /var/lib/dbus/machine-id, the value of the kernel command line option container_uuid, the KVM DMI product_uuid or the devicetree vm,uuid (on KVM systems), the Xen hypervisor uuid, and finally a randomly generated UUID. systemd.machine_id=firmware can be set to generate the machine ID from the firmware.

After the machine ID is established, systemd1 will attempt to save it to /etc/machine-id. If this fails, it will attempt to bind-mount a temporary file over /etc/machine-id. It is an error if the file system is read-only and does not contain a (possibly empty) /etc/machine-id file.
systemd-machine-id-commit.service8 will attempt to write the machine ID to the file system if /etc/machine-id or /etc/ are read-only during early boot but become writable later on.

refsect1.title: First Boot Semantics
refsect1.para: /etc/machine-id is used to decide whether a boot is the first one. The rules are as follows:

listitem.para: The kernel command argument systemd.condition_first_boot= may be used to override the autodetection logic, see kernel-command-line7.

Otherwise, if /etc/machine-id does not exist, this is a first boot. During early boot, systemd will write uninitialized\n to this file and overmount a temporary file which contains the actual machine ID. Later (after first-boot-complete.target has been reached), the real machine ID will be written to disk.
If /etc/machine-id contains the string uninitialized, a boot is also considered the first boot. The same mechanism as above applies.

If /etc/machine-id exists and is empty, a boot is not considered the first boot. systemd will still bind-mount a file containing the actual machine-id over it and later try to commit it to disk (if /etc/ is writable).
If /etc/machine-id already contains a valid machine-id, this is not a first boot.

refsect1.para: If according to the above rules a first boot is detected, units with ConditionFirstBoot=yes will be run and systemd will perform additional initialization steps, in particular presetting units.

refsect1.title: Cloned Systems
refsect1.para: When a system is installed by cloning a disk image or a virtual machine that already carries a populated /etc/machine-id, every clone inherits the very same machine ID, which defeats the uniqueness the ID is supposed to provide. The preferred way to avoid this is to not ship a populated machine ID in the first place, i.e. to leave /etc/machine-id empty (or missing) in the image, as described in "Initialization" above: each clone then acquires an ID of its own on first boot. Note that this is only sufficient if the image carries no other source of the golden image's identity either. A regular /var/lib/dbus/machine-id — the shape dbus-uuidgen creates — and a baked-in system.machine_id credential are both consulted first, and would hand every clone the same ID; clear them, or make the D-Bus file a symlink to /etc/machine-id. An explicit systemd.machine_id= in the image's boot loader entries or /etc/kernel/cmdline defeats it outright: it takes precedence over the file entirely, and the service manager writes its value into /etc/machine-id on every boot, so it has to be dropped from the image too.

If the image cannot be prepared that way, or if the clone has already been made, a new identity may be assigned with the --force switch of systemd-machine-id-setup1, which replaces the current ID with a freshly generated random one. Ideally this is done offline, on the mounted (but not booted) clone:
--image= works the same way on a disk image. If the offline route is not available, the running clone can be reprovisioned as well, but it has to be rebooted afterwards:

The reboot is required in the online case only, because the machine ID is cached by every process that has read it, including the service manager itself, hence a running system keeps using the old ID until it is restarted. Stale copies of the old ID that would otherwise be handed back the next time the machine ID is initialized — /run/machine-id and a regular /var/lib/dbus/machine-id — are rewritten by --force itself, on a best-effort basis: one that exists but cannot be written is reported as a warning without failing the run, while one that is simply absent is not reported at all. Symlinks among them are never rewritten, whatever they point at: one aimed at /etc/machine-id already resolves to the new ID and needs nothing, but one aimed elsewhere still holds the old identity and is the operator's to deal with.

If the clone's boot loader entries carry a systemd.machine_id= kernel command line parameter with an explicit ID, it has to be dropped or updated as well. As described above such a value takes precedence over /etc/machine-id, and the service manager writes it back to that file on every boot, so the reboot mandated above would silently restore the old ID. A value of firmware does not have that effect, as it leaves the file itself authoritative. Online, --force refuses to run while a parameter carrying an explicit ID is set; offline it cannot see the clone's command line, so this is on the operator.
Note that changing the machine ID discards or invalidates state that is keyed by it, and does not rewrite identifiers already derived from it. Before proceeding, in particular consider the following:

listitem.para: The host key for encrypted credentials, i.e. /var/lib/systemd/credential.secret, see systemd-creds1, is bound to the machine ID: the first read that sees a mismatching ID deletes the file. Any data encrypted with it — for example via systemd-creds encrypt or LoadCredentialEncrypted= — is then permanently undecryptable, and services relying on such credentials fail. Note that re-encrypting beforehand does not help, as the new ciphertext is bound to the very secret that is about to be discarded: decrypt anything worth keeping to plaintext with systemd-creds decrypt before the machine ID is changed, and encrypt it again once the new ID is in effect. Note that systemd-creds1 takes no --root=, so it always uses the host's secret and machine ID: in the offline workflow above the decryption has to be done from inside the clone while it is still booted with the old ID, i.e. before running --force against it.

The machine ID is measured into PCR 15 by systemd-pcrextend8, and systemd-pcrlock's default policy set covers that PCR. Once it changes, LUKS volumes enrolled against PCR 15 with systemd-cryptenroll1 or bound to a pcrlock policy stop unlocking until they are re-enrolled or the policy is regenerated — which for anything unlocked after systemd-pcrmachine.service, such as /home/, has to be arranged before the reboot.

GPT auto-discovery of the /var/ partition matches its partition UUID against an HMAC keyed by the machine ID, see systemd-gpt-auto-generator8. Such a partition is no longer picked up until its partition UUID is recalculated from the new ID and written into the partition table. Note that systemd-id128 var-partition-uuid always keys the HMAC with the machine ID of the system it runs on and takes no --root=, so in the offline workflow above it has to be run from within the clone once it has booted, not on the host.

Persistent journal files live in a directory named after the machine ID, see systemd-journald.service8. Log data collected before the change does not merely stay behind in the old directory, it stops being visible to plain journalctl1, which only opens the directory matching the current ID; reaching it afterwards takes --merge or an explicit --directory=/var/log/journal/OLD-ID.

Unless /etc/kernel/entry-token pins it, the boot loader entry token defaults to the machine ID, see the --entry-token= option of kernel-install8. Boot entries and the kernel directory below the boot partition are then named after the old ID and are orphaned by the change: they are no longer refreshed, and no longer removed when the corresponding kernel is. Pinning the token in /etc/kernel/entry-token beforehand avoids this.

Network identity is derived from the machine ID: the DHCP DUID defaults to the DUID-EN type computed from it, so after the change the host presents a different DUID and loses its leases and reservations; stable-privacy IPv6 addresses change with it. Under MACAddressPolicy=persistent the machine ID is also mixed into the interface MAC address, but only for links without a usable permanent hardware address — hardware that has one, as most does, keeps it, see systemd.link5. Anything keyed to these upstream — DHCP reservations, firewall rules, 802.1X allow-lists — needs updating too.
Application-specific IDs obtained via sd_id128_get_machine_app_specific3 change along with the machine ID.

refsect1.title: Relation to OSF UUIDs
refsect1.para: Note that the machine ID historically is not an OSF UUID as defined by RFC 4122, nor a Microsoft GUID; however, starting with systemd v30, newly generated machine IDs do qualify as Variant 1 Version 4 UUIDs, as per RFC 4122.

refsect1.title: History
refsect1.para: The simple configuration file format of /etc/machine-id originates in the /var/lib/dbus/machine-id file introduced by D-Bus. In fact, this latter file might be a symlink to /etc/machine-id.
